title: RSA
summary: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem whose security rests on the presumed hardness of factoring the product of two large primes, combined with modular exponentiation over that product. A key pair consists of a modulus derived from two secret primes, a public exponent usually 65537, and a private exponent derived through the extended Euclidean algorithm. RSA supports both encryption and digital signatures, and it is normally used inside a padding or encoding scheme rather than on raw data, because textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable. Encryption uses OAEP padding; signatures use PSS or the older PKCS#1 v1.5 scheme, and the padding choice is where most real-world breaks have occurred. Practical risks include small key sizes that are within reach of well-resourced factoring efforts, shared or non-random primes generated by faulty entropy sources, Bleichenbacher-style padding oracle attacks against v1.5 encryption, and signature verification code that ignores algorithm identifiers or accepts the wrong hash. Signing is also much slower than verifying, which shapes how RSA is deployed in certificate chains and protocol handshakes. Throughout their lifecycle, RSA keys must be protected against exfiltration, rotated before weakness accumulates, and retired with their certificates, which is why hardware modules and inventory of key material are operational controls rather than cryptographic footnotes.
objectives: Explain the mathematical structure of an RSA key pair and why factoring the modulus compromises both confidentiality and authenticity.
Distinguish OAEP encryption padding from PSS and PKCS#1 v1.5 signature schemes, and state when each is acceptable.
Describe how a padding oracle attack against RSA encryption is exploited and how constant-time error handling mitigates it.
Identify weak key generation in an asset inventory, including undersized moduli and duplicated or non-random primes.
Interpret certificate chain and signature algorithm fields during a review of TLS or code-signing infrastructure.
Assess the migration path away from RSA towards elliptic curve and post-quantum signature schemes in a live environment.

beginner.definition: RSA is a public key method for encryption and digital signatures. The name comes from its three inventors. It uses two linked keys: a public key anyone may see and a private key you keep secret. Its safety rests on one idea. Multiplying two large prime numbers is easy, but splitting the answer back into those primes is hard.
beginner.whyItMatters: RSA has protected the internet for decades, and you still meet it in certificates, secure connections and signed software. It also shows the cost of getting cryptography wrong. Most real RSA breaks did not come from difficult maths. They came from weak random numbers, keys that were too short, or error messages that leaked small clues. Protecting the private key is the other half of the job.
howItWorks: The computer picks two very large prime numbers and multiplies them together.
That product becomes the public part of the key, and it is shared freely.
The two primes stay secret and form the private key, which must never be shared.
To encrypt, the sender scrambles data with the public key and some padding rules.
Only the matching private key can unscramble it back into readable data.
To sign, the owner scrambles a short fingerprint of the message with the private key.
beginner.example: Imagine a padlock that anyone can snap shut, but only you hold the key that opens it. A friend puts a secret note in a box, locks it with your open padlock and sends it. Anyone can copy the open padlock and send you locked boxes, but nobody can open them. If someone ever copies your key, or your key is made from a guessable number, every box is exposed.
takeaways: RSA uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock or sign.
Its strength depends on key length and on truly random prime numbers.
Use modern padding and never reveal detailed errors, because clues help attackers.
